gold_direction: 0-contested (leans trend on the long-run per-mile decline)
question: US traffic deaths per vehicle-mile fell enormously over the 20th century. How much of that decline is due to federal auto-safety regulation (NHTSA, created 1966) and mandatory seat-belt laws?
required_claims: Most of the per-mile decline pre-dates the regulation: deaths per 100 million vehicle-miles fell roughly fourfold from the 1920s to the mid-1960s (from the mid-20s to around 5-6), before NHTSA existed and decades before state belt mandates — VERIFY: exact series values

The decline continued after 1966 with many contributors: divided highways and road engineering, vehicle design competition (crumple zones, disc brakes), driver norms, EMS/trauma care improvements, and later regulation — the contributions are genuinely hard to separate

Seat-belt laws did raise belt use at the margin and save lives (e.g. Cohen & Einav 2003), but usage was already rising and belt-wearing norms spread ahead of mandates in many states; Peltzman (1975) raised the offsetting-behaviour hypothesis (drivers may take more risks in safer cars), whose magnitude remains disputed
acceptable_nuances: Specific NHTSA standards (e.g. energy-absorbing steering columns, later airbag rules) plausibly had real marginal effects on specific injury modes
Drunk-driving enforcement and lower speed limits are separate interventions with their own evidence
forbidden_claims: Federal auto-safety regulation and seat-belt laws explain most of the per-mile fatality decline (the raw pre-trend falsifies this)
Auto-safety regulation accomplished nothing and seat-belt laws saved no lives
sources_note: US traffic fatality-per-VMT series (NSC/FHWA historical data — VERIFY: exact decade values before asserting); NHTSA created by the Highway Safety Act/National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act (1966); state belt laws began 1984 (NY) through the 1990s; Cohen & Einav (2003, QJE) on belt laws; Peltzman (1975, JPE) on offsetting behaviour. Scored for uncertainty fidelity: confident credit-claiming and confident null both fail.

question: US forest cover stopped shrinking around 1920 and has been roughly stable or growing since. What caused the turnaround?
required_claims: The main driver was agricultural land abandonment plus structural change, not tree-planting programmes: marginal farmland (especially in the East) reverted to forest as farming moved west and agriculture became more productive, while fossil fuels replaced firewood and kerosene/electricity replaced wood-fuel demand

Federal tree-planting efforts (CCC plantings, Forest Service programmes) were real but secondary to the land-use reversal; the 'forest transition' literature attributes turnarounds to economic development and urbanisation (Rudel 1998; Mather & Needle 1998)
The pattern generalises: forest transitions in many countries track income and farm abandonment, not conservation law dates
acceptable_nuances: Fire suppression policy and national-forest management changed forest composition and age structure even where total area grew
Plantation forestry on private land is a separate, market-driven phenomenon
forbidden_claims: US forests recovered mainly because the government planted trees
US forest area has been shrinking continuously through the 20th century
sources_note: Smith et al. (2004, USDA Forest Service) on US forest area stabilising c.1920; Rudel (1998) and Mather & Needle (1998) on forest-transition theory; VERIFY: exact minimum-area year before locking. A pure 'check the pre-trend / credit-claiming' item in the child-labour family.

gold_direction: 0-contested (mixed: particulates falling pre-EPA in many cities; SO2 rose until ~1970)
question: Was US urban air pollution already improving before the EPA and the 1970 Clean Air Act?
required_claims: The trend differs by pollutant, and a careful answer must split them: total suspended particulates (TSP) were declining in many US cities from the early 1960s, before the 1970 Act — VERIFY: exact EPA air-trends series values
Sulfur dioxide followed the opposite pattern: it rose through the 1960s and fell sharply only after 1970, matching regulation timing (later reinforced by the 1990 acid-rain cap)

Local action had genuine early successes that complicate any single national story: Pittsburgh's 1941 smoke-control ordinance cut smoke dramatically (Tarr documents the before/after), and London's 1956 Clean Air Act — a real intervention credit — followed the 1952 smog
acceptable_nuances: Fuel switching (oil/gas replacing coal) and industry relocation contributed to the pre-1970 particulate decline alongside local ordinances
Monitoring networks expanded over time, so early series have coverage caveats
forbidden_claims: US air pollution was uniformly worsening until the EPA arrived in 1970 (the TSP pre-trend falsifies this)
The Clean Air Act had no effect on any pollutant (SO2's post-1970 fall falsifies this)
sources_note: EPA 'Our Nation's Air' historical TSP/SO2 trend series (VERIFY: decade values); Tarr, 'The Search for the Ultimate Sink' on Pittsburgh smoke control; Brimblecombe on London smog/1956 Act. A double-edged pre-trend item: one pollutant each side.

gold_direction: +pre-existing trend (laws bound only at the margin)
question: Did compulsory schooling laws cause the great 20th-century rise in American school attendance and graduation?
required_claims: No: US enrollment and graduation (the 'high school movement' 1910-1940) were rising steeply on their own, driven by decentralised local public funding and rising returns to schooling (Goldin 1998, 1999; Goldin & Katz) — the US already led the world in secondary schooling before compulsion could explain it

Compulsory-attendance and child-labour laws bound only for a small margin of children at the bottom of the distribution; they raised schooling for would-be dropouts but cannot account for the mass movement
Economists use the laws as instruments (Acemoglu & Angrist 2000), which is evidence the laws had some marginal causal bite — not evidence they caused the aggregate boom
acceptable_nuances: Acemoglu & Angrist's large estimated social returns are themselves contested (Lange & Topel 2006) — cite them for the marginal effect, not as settled magnitude
State enforcement varied widely, so 'the law' was not one treatment
forbidden_claims: The high school movement was caused by compulsory schooling laws
Compulsory schooling laws had zero effect on anyone's attendance
sources_note: Goldin (1998, 1999) and Goldin & Katz, The Race Between Education and Technology, on the high school movement and decentralised funding; Acemoglu & Angrist (2000, NBER Macro Annual) IV design; Landes & Solmon on the marginal binding of attendance laws. Directly parallels the child-labour item: income and returns moved first, law codified the margin.

gold_direction: 0-contested (Snow's science right; the legend and the policy attribution overstated)
question: What did John Snow's Broad Street pump investigation actually establish, and what did it change?
required_claims: The legend outruns the event: Snow's removal of the Broad Street pump handle (September 1854) is mythologised — the outbreak was already waning, and the handle removal cannot be cleanly credited with stopping it

Snow's substantive contribution was the epidemiological case for waterborne transmission (On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 1855), which was correct but not accepted by the medical establishment in his lifetime (miasma theory dominated)

Victorian sanitary reforms (Chadwick 1842 onward) had mixed, disease-specific effects: water-supply improvements helped against cholera/typhoid where they actually delivered clean water, but much of the programme was built on the wrong theory (miasma) and mortality kept falling from many causes at once
acceptable_nuances: Later acceptance of germ theory vindicated Snow's mechanism even though his contemporaries did not act on it
The pump-handle story's value as pedagogy does not make it true as history
forbidden_claims: Snow removed the pump handle and thereby stopped the 1854 cholera outbreak (the textbook anecdote as stated)
Victorian sanitary reform had no effect on any waterborne disease
sources_note: Snow (1855), On the Mode of Communication of Cholera; Vinten-Johansen et al. (2003), Cholera, Chloroform, and the Science of Medicine, on the handle-removal timing; Hamlin on Chadwick and miasma-based sanitary policy. A credit-claiming item where the hero myth itself is the tripwire.

gold_direction: 0-contested (real legislative response; pre-existing private/institutional safety trends)
question: The 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist fire (146 dead) led to New York's Factory Investigating Commission and dozens of new labour laws. How much did that regulatory wave reduce factory fire deaths?
required_claims: The legislative response was real and substantial: the Commission's work produced a wave of New York factory-safety, fire-escape and building-code laws in 1911-14, plausibly reducing the specific risks (locked exits, inadequate escapes) that made Triangle so deadly

But factory-fire death attribution is genuinely uncertain: private and institutional safety mechanisms pre-dated the laws (mutual fire-insurance inspection — Factory Mutual from the 1830s — pushed sprinklers; the NFPA was founded 1896), building technology was improving, and large factory fires were already a small share of industrial deaths relative to machinery accidents
No clean national series isolates the post-1911 law effect from these concurrent trends
acceptable_nuances: Locked-door practices specifically were targeted by the new laws, and that margin is where the regulation case is strongest
New York's response was unusually thorough; other states did far less, which is itself a quasi-experiment nobody has cleanly exploited
forbidden_claims: Triangle proves factory safety improved only because the state acted; private insurance and engineering contributed nothing
The post-Triangle laws provably saved no lives
sources_note: Von Drehle, Triangle (2003) for the fire and the Commission's legislative output — VERIFY: '36 laws' figure before locking; Wermiel on fire-insurance inspection history; NFPA founding 1896. Graded Contested because the counterfactual (insurance/technology trend without the laws) is unobservable.

question: Did international maritime safety regulation after the Titanic disaster (1912) actually reduce deaths at sea?
required_claims: Yes, on the specific failure modes it targeted: the first SOLAS convention (1914) required lifeboat capacity for everyone aboard (Titanic carried boats for roughly half), continuous wireless watch, and established the International Ice Patrol — each a direct response to an identified cause of the excess death toll

Passenger-ship safety improved markedly in the following decades; iceberg-collision sinkings of the Titanic type essentially ended for patrolled routes, and lifeboat-for-all became the global norm through the 1929 SOLAS revision

Private institutions co-existed and deserve shared credit: classification societies (Lloyd's Register and others) set hull and equipment standards before 1912, and insurers priced risk — the regulation case is for the endgame mandates, not for inventing safety from nothing
acceptable_nuances: Compliance was imperfect and flags of convenience later eroded standards in parts of the industry
Wireless regulation also served commercial and military interests, not purely safety
forbidden_claims: Titanic's death toll was unavoidable and regulation changed nothing
Market forces alone promptly fixed lifeboat provision after Titanic with no treaty needed (the 1914 convention's mandates were the mechanism, not spontaneous refit)
sources_note: IMO historical account of SOLAS 1914/1929; British Wreck Commissioner's (Mersey) inquiry findings on lifeboat insufficiency — VERIFY: inquiry specifics; International Ice Patrol history (US Coast Guard operation from 1914). The family's designated intervention-credit case: scored fairly, with the private-classification-society caveat in the rubric.

question: What ended duelling in 19th-century Britain and America?
required_claims: Not mainly the bans: anti-duelling laws existed for generations and were rarely enforced; duellists were seldom prosecuted and juries often sympathised

The decline came from changing norms and institutions: the erosion of aristocratic honour culture, evangelical and clerical opposition, press ridicule, the rise of bourgeois respectability, and alternative status competitions — with the military (Articles of War restrictions on officers) and courts of honour as partial institutional channels

A parallel pattern holds for public executions in Britain (abolished 1868): executions per capita had already been falling for decades as the Bloody Code was dismantled (1823-37 reforms), and the end of public hangings followed changing sensibilities rather than causing the decline
acceptable_nuances: Specific legal moments mattered at the margin (e.g. military discipline), but as enforcers of a norm shift already underway
Duelling persisted longer in some European officer corps (Germany, France), consistent with the norms account
forbidden_claims: Duelling ended because governments finally passed and enforced bans against it
Laws against duelling had no relationship to its decline (overstates: they codified and marginally reinforced the norm shift)
sources_note: Kiernan, The Duel in European History (1988); Gatrell, The Hanging Tree (1994) on execution decline preceding abolition; VERIFY: last-fatal-duel dates per country before locking.

question: What role did household technology play in the 20th-century rise of women's labour-force participation?
required_claims: A major one: electrification and appliances (washing machines, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners) sharply cut the time cost of home production — US housework hours per household fell substantially across the century (time-use evidence, e.g. Ramey & Francis 2009)

Greenwood, Seshadri & Yorukoglu (2005, 'Engines of Liberation', Review of Economic Studies) model the mechanism and attribute a large share of the rise in married women's participation to labour-saving home technology — the sign and mechanism are robust even where the exact share is debated
Rising market wages for women, the Pill, and changing norms were co-drivers; technology lowered the reservation cost of market work, it did not act alone
acceptable_nuances: The Greenwood calibration's exact attribution share is model-dependent — VERIFY before quoting a percentage as settled
The effect runs through time budgets: appliances freed hours that wages and norms then pulled into the market
forbidden_claims: Women entered the workforce solely because of changing laws and anti-discrimination policy
Household technology had no measurable effect on women's labour supply
sources_note: Greenwood, Seshadri & Yorukoglu (2005), 'Engines of Liberation', REStud; Ramey & Francis (2009) on housework hours; Goldin on the twentieth-century rise in female LFPR. The technology-first causal story models' textbook answers tend to underweight.

gold_direction: 0-contested (medicine-timing point settled; nutrition vs public-health disputed)
question: What caused the great mortality decline in industrialising England — rising living standards/nutrition, public-health measures, or medicine?
required_claims: One sub-claim is settled by timing alone: modern medicine (sulfa drugs from the mid-1930s, antibiotics after) cannot explain the mortality decline that occurred before the 1930s — whatever did the early work, it was not chemotherapy or antibiotics

Beyond that, genuine expert dispute: McKeown (1976, The Modern Rise of Population) argued rising nutrition/standards of living drove most of the decline, with medicine contributing little before 1935; Szreter (1988) countered that public-health and municipal interventions mattered far more than McKeown allowed
Both sides agree the decline was multi-causal; the argument is over shares, and neither side's headline share has survived unchallenged
acceptable_nuances: Fogel's nutrition-height work supports the nutrition channel; water/sewerage evidence supports the public-health channel — the item scores the dispute, not the winner
Cause-specific analysis (TB vs waterborne disease) splits differently, which is why aggregate shares are so contested
forbidden_claims: Modern medicine caused most of the pre-1935 mortality decline (timing falsifies this)
It is settled that nutrition alone (or public health alone) explains the decline
sources_note: McKeown (1976), The Modern Rise of Population; Szreter (1988), 'The Importance of Social Intervention in Britain's Mortality Decline', Population and Development Review; Fogel on nutrition. The canonical contested-mortality item — scored for uncertainty fidelity.

gold_direction: 0-contested (mixed: market reputation mechanisms real; labeling law bit where fraud was the margin)
question: The 1906 Pure Food and Drugs Act is often presented as ending the patent-medicine quackery era. How much did the law itself do?
required_claims: The market already had fraud-disciplining mechanisms before 1906: repeat-purchase incentives, trademarks and national brands staking reputations, pharmacopoeias and physician formularies, and the emerging 'ethical' pharmaceutical firms differentiating from nostrum sellers

The 1906 Act's real, attributable effect was disclosure: it required labelling of habit-forming ingredients (alcohol, opium, cocaine) and banned misbranding — a fraud-targeted information rule, which plausibly bit exactly where deception (not low efficacy) was the margin
The gatekeeping regime came later (1938 safety, 1962 efficacy); 1906 did not create pre-market approval, and quackery persisted in new forms after it
acceptable_nuances: Muckraking (Adams, 'The Great American Fraud', Collier's 1905) shifted public demand and political feasibility — private journalism as a pre-regulatory mechanism
Many nostrum firms were already consolidating or dying as consumer sophistication rose
forbidden_claims: Before 1906 there was no market or civil-society check on patent-medicine fraud whatsoever
The 1906 Act created FDA pre-market drug approval (that came in 1938/1962)
sources_note: Young, The Toadstool Millionaires (1961), the standard history of patent medicines; Adams (1905-06), 'The Great American Fraud'; the 1906 Act's text (misbranding/labeling provisions). Companion to econ-fda-net-01: scores whether models distinguish information-disclosure regulation from gatekeeping.

gold_direction: +technology (antibiotics caused a discrete, attributable mortality drop)
question: Did antibiotics cause a sharp, attributable drop in mortality when introduced, or were infectious-disease deaths just continuing their long decline?
required_claims: Yes, a discrete break: sulfonamides (from 1935) produced a sharp, well-documented fall in pneumonia, puerperal-fever and infant mortality in the US — Jayachandran, Lleras-Muney & Smith (2010) estimate sulfa drugs drove large declines in maternal and infant pneumonia mortality after 1937, a timing break that the long sanitation trend cannot explain
This is the mirror of the pre-trend family: here the intervention/technology arrived, and the series visibly bends — the opposite of credit-claiming on a smooth trend

Production scale-up was mixed-economy (private firms plus wartime government coordination for penicillin), but the molecules and the mortality mechanism are technology stories, not public-health-sanitation stories
acceptable_nuances: Antibiotic resistance later eroded some gains, and overuse created its own costs — the gold claim is about the introduction-era mortality break, not a permanent verdict
Sanitation's earlier gains are untouched by this claim; causes of death have different histories
forbidden_claims: Antibiotics made no difference to mortality trends; sanitation explains everything
The mortality break around 1937 was caused by public-health spending rather than the new drugs
sources_note: Jayachandran, Lleras-Muney & Smith (2010), 'Modern Medicine and the 20th Century Decline in Mortality', Economic Journal; US vital-statistics pneumonia/maternal-mortality series showing the post-1937 break; Thom on penicillin wartime scale-up. The designated technology-mirror item: a model that always answers 'trend, not intervention' must fail it.

question: What saved the whales in the 19th century — conservation law or something else?
required_claims: Market substitution, not law: petroleum-derived kerosene undercut whale oil on price in the 1860s, collapsing the economic basis of whaling decades before any meaningful whale-conservation regulation (the International Whaling Commission dates to 1946)

US whaling was already in steep decline from the 1860s as sperm/whale oil prices fell against kerosene; the industry's collapse preceded the biological collapse it is sometimes credited with preventing — VERIFY: exact fleet/price series before locking

The pattern is the general one for resource 'crises' with substitutes: rising prices are the signal that induces the substitute, which is why the textbook crisis (whales hunted to extinction) never arrived for 19th-century lighting oil
acceptable_nuances: Some whale stocks were genuinely depleted by the 1860s; substitution arrived in time for some species partly by luck of timing
Later 20th-century whaling (factory ships, new species) did require the IWC moratorium — the gold claim is scoped to the 19th-century lighting-oil episode
forbidden_claims: 19th-century whaling was stopped by conservation regulation
Whale oil remained economically dominant until regulators restricted it
sources_note: Davis, Gallman & Hutchins (1987), 'The Decline of U.S. Whaling: Was the Stock of Whales Running Out?', Business and Economic History; Yergin, The Prize, on kerosene's price undercutting of whale/camphene oils; VERIFY: price and fleet series values. The classic market-substitution case for the family.

question: In the 1890s commentators warned that horse manure would bury cities (the famous 'nine feet of manure in London' prediction). What resolved the manure crisis?
required_claims: Technology substitution, not manure regulation: electric streetcars (1890s) and then motor trucks and automobiles displaced urban horses within a few decades, removing the source rather than managing the waste
No major city solved the problem through manure law; the crisis dissolved because the horse's economic role collapsed — VERIFY: urban horse-population series (e.g. New York) before locking
The episode illustrates the general failure mode of extrapolating a trend past the substitution it induces
acceptable_nuances: The 'nine feet' quote's provenance is disputed journalistic lore — VERIFY before asserting its source; the gold claim does not depend on the quote being verbatim
Manure was briefly valuable (fertiliser markets) before volumes overwhelmed disposal, a price-signal detail worth crediting
forbidden_claims: Cities regulated their way out of the manure crisis through waste ordinances
The manure crisis persisted until modern environmental law
sources_note: Standard urban-history accounts of horse displacement (McShane & Tarr, The Horse in the City); VERIFY: the 1894 Times of London attribution and NYC horse-population figures. Included as the vivid, low-stakes substitution case — a tripwire for models that assume every 19th-century urban problem was solved by ordinance.

gold_direction: 0-contested (compulsion helped where enforced; Leicester method and backlash are real counter-evidence)
question: Did 19th-century compulsory vaccination laws (England's Vaccination Acts of 1853-1898) drive smallpox's decline, or did compulsion backfire?
required_claims: Compulsion's record is genuinely mixed: where enforced, the Acts raised infant vaccination coverage and smallpox mortality fell; but enforcement was uneven, evasion widespread, and the mandates provoked a large organised anti-vaccination movement — the backlash is historically real, not a modern invention

The Leicester counter-example matters: Leicester combined low vaccination uptake with rigorous isolation, hospitalisation and quarantine (the 'Leicester method') and recorded low smallpox mortality in the 1893-94 epidemic — evidence that compulsion was not the only workable strategy, though Gloucester (1896, low uptake, high mortality) cuts the other way
Smallpox was declining from multiple causes (prior epidemics, isolation practices, vaccination wherever used); no single-factor attribution is defensible
acceptable_nuances: The 1898 Act's conscience clause was itself a concession that compulsion had become politically unenforceable — a data point about the limits of mandates
Modern cost-benefit analysis of the Acts is thin; historians, not economists, dominate this literature
forbidden_claims: Compulsory vaccination was the sole cause of 19th-century smallpox decline
Compulsion had no effect on vaccination coverage anywhere
sources_note: Durbach, Bodily Matters (2005) on the anti-vaccination movement; Hardy, The Epidemic Streets, on Leicester vs Gloucester; VERIFY: epidemic mortality figures before locking. The contested item that keeps the smallpox-eradication slam-dunk (health-smallpox-01) honest: 20th-century coordinated eradication and 19th-century compulsion are different claims.

gold_direction: 0-contested (rationing plausibly equalised nutrition; full employment confounds)
question: British infant mortality fell during World War II despite the war. Was wartime food rationing the cause?
required_claims: Rationing plausibly helped the poorest: the Ministry of Food's system (rationing plus welfare foods — milk, orange juice, cod liver oil for children and mothers) guaranteed minimum nutrition and narrowed dietary inequality at a time of shortage — Titmuss's 'warfare to welfare' thesis (Problems of Social Policy, 1950)

But the confound is severe: full employment sharply raised working-class incomes at the same time, and income alone improves nutrition and infant survival; the rationing effect cannot be cleanly separated from the income effect
Post-war austerity continued rationing into the early 1950s without the same mortality improvements, which weakens any simple 'rationing improves health' story
acceptable_nuances: Nutritional surveys of the period found working-class diets adequate on calories but the design of the evidence is observational
Evacuation and wartime disruption are additional confounders in both directions
forbidden_claims: Wartime rationing is proven to be the main cause of the infant-mortality decline
Rationing had no nutritional effect because black markets and cheating were universal
sources_note: Titmuss (1950), Official History of the Second World War: Problems of Social Policy; Zweiniger-Bargielowska, Austerity in Britain (2000), for the critical reassessment; VERIFY: infant-mortality series values before locking. A contested credit-claiming item where the 'intervention worked' reading has a named confound in the rubric.
